1:
When the ruin described here happened is the first question. Adam Clarke says it was plainly written when the temple was in ruins, Jerusalem burnt and the prophets scattered, but that it is not clear whether the desolations refer to the days of Nebuchadnezzar or to the destruction under the Romans about the seventieth year of the Christian era; Calmet, he notes, inclines to the former. John Calvin settles only the negative half: it cannot be ascribed to David, since in his time there was no ground for mourning over such a wasted condition of the Church, and though others allege that he foretold it by the spirit of prophecy, it is probable many psalms were composed after his death and this is one of them. Keil and Delitzsch argue from style and echo, finding the old Asaphic impress in the contemplation of Israel as a flock and in the fondness for retrospect over its early history, and noting how closely Jeremiah stands to this psalm, one passage being repeated almost word for word while the lament that there is no prophet any more sounds much like Lamentations. Charles Ellicott finds the best explanation of the third verse in a later account of Jerusalem lying void as a wilderness.

Whether the opening question is a proper one divides the entry. C.H. Spurgeon says no. It is our wisdom under chastisement to enquire wherefore God contends with us, and a church in a forsaken condition must not sit still in apathy; yet the enquiry of the text is faulty, implying two mistakes, since both its questions admit only a negative reply. Grief in its distraction, he says, asks strange questions and surmises impossible terrors. Matthew Henry is gentler about the same liberty: we hope it is not too great a one, since Christ upon the cross cried out that God had forsaken him; and God’s people must not think that because they are cast down they are cast off, or that a seeming rejection for a time is a real one for ever. John Gill puts the fault on unbelief, which read the hidings of God’s face as a casting off when it was so only in appearance. Charles Ellicott sharpens the complaint instead, rendering the line why hast thou never ceased abandoning us.

What is asked to be remembered is described in religious and political terms at once. Charles Ellicott observes that purchased, with redeemed beside it, shows the song at the Red Sea was in the writer’s mind, and that congregation presents the people in its religious aspect while the rod of thine inheritance presents it in its political character — the rod being not a shepherd’s crook but the staff of a tribal prince, which passes into a term for the tribe itself. John Wesley names that tribe as Judah, chosen for God’s inheritance and for the birth of the Messiah, the calamity having chiefly befallen it and Benjamin. John Gill allows the allusion to the redemption out of Egypt but holds the purchase was not in reality made till the blood of Christ was shed.

The last plea is a call to come and look. Charles Ellicott prefers lift thy steps, a poetical expression inviting God to hasten and view the desolation, and would render the noun either ruins which must be ever ruins or ruins of splendour. John Gill reads it as arise, hasten and come and see, though some, with the Targum, take it as a prayer for the destruction of the church’s enemies. Augustine of Hippo works from the title, since Asaph means congregation, and asks what sort of Israel is meant — not of the chaff but of the grain, not of the broken branches but of those strengthened, for not all that are of Israel are Israelites; and by that reckoning all are Israelites who follow the faith of our father Abraham.
4:
The roaring in the sanctuary is described alike and located differently. Charles Ellicott paints the scene: instead of the voices of priest and choir there have been heard the brutal cries of the heathen shouting at their work of destruction, like lions roaring over their prey; or, if the next clause refers to military ensigns, a picture of a wild soldiery exulting round the emblem of their triumph. Adam Clarke reads the verse of the Babylonians and sets down the record from the histories — the city broken up, Zedekiah’s sons slain before his eyes and his own put out, the captain of the guard burning the house of the Lord, the walls broken down, the pillars of brass and the brazen sea broken in pieces and the metal carried to Babylon. He adds that a people who would not so much as touch a Gentile were now obliged to mingle with the most profane. John Gill takes the congregations for churches gathered in Gospel order, and the roaring for Satan and antichrist, whose mouth is the mouth of a lion. John Wesley keeps it plain: they roared in a way of triumph, in the places where God’s people used to assemble for worship.

What the ensigns were is a smaller crux. Charles Ellicott observes that the Hebrew for ensigns and for signs is one word, and suspects the poet meant to write some word meaning idols but avoided it from dislike of naming the abominable things, so that instead of writing that they placed their idols as signs he wrote that they placed their signs as signs. John Wesley calls them monuments of victory, and Adam Clarke renders the line that they set up their standards in the place of ours, our own being no longer to be seen.

The verse about the axes is the hardest in the psalm, and Charles Ellicott says the Authorised Version has entirely mistaken it, though unlike the older versions it has at least the merit of being intelligible. Literally the words run that he is known like one lifting up axes on high against a thicket of trees, generally taken to mean that the destroyers went to work like woodcutters in a forest, the carved pillars being no more to them than trees to fell. But this, he says, does not read like Hebrew, and it loses the contrast the poet intended between the signs of the heathen and the signs of Israel; read the verb as a plural with the Greek and the contrast comes out plainly — they set up their idols as signs, and these signs are known in the lifting up on high, whereas we see not our signs. He then supplies the comparison the English omits: as in a thicket of trees with axes, so now they break down all the carved work with axes and hammers — the carving of the temple having represented palm-trees and flowers, which makes the image very appropriate.

John Wesley and John Gill read the passage as a contrast of honour and contempt rather than a crux. The temple was so noble a structure, Wesley says, that it was a great honour to be employed in the meanest part of the work, though but in cutting down the trees of Lebanon; and Gill sets the two moments side by side, that formerly it was an honour to fell a tree for the building, but now the fine carved work Solomon made was demolished at once in a rude and furious manner. Who did it he leaves partly open, naming the Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar, the Syrians under Antiochus and the Romans under Vespasian, and preferring the first. John Wesley offers a philological argument for that date: the words for axes and hammers are not Hebrew but Chaldee, pointing to the time when the Chaldeans brought in their language along with their arms.
7:
The burning is stated flatly and then qualified. John Gill allows the clause to be turned about, either that they cast fire into the sanctuary or the sanctuary into the fire, and takes it either way for its utter destruction. Charles Ellicott prefers the second order and thinks the phrase probably hyperbolical, purporting to express the vastness of the conflagration, and adds from a later history that when the temple came to be restored the gates were found to have been burnt.

The synagogues are the real difficulty, and the two commentators who face it take opposite courses. Adam Clarke begins from the chronology: it is supposed that there were no synagogues in the land until after the Babylonish captivity, and if so, how could the Chaldeans burn any? He answers by widening the word, which may be taken more generally for any place where religious assemblies were held — and such places existed long before, since Elisha kept one at his house on the sabbaths and new moons, and meetings were held at the house of Ezekiel. This, he notes, is the only place in the Old Testament where the word synagogue appears; and wherever God had met with patriarch or prophet and a memorial was preserved, there was such a place, all of which the Chaldeans would destroy in pursuance of their design to extinguish the Jewish religion. He measures the policy by imagining it at home: how soon would Christianity be destroyed in England if all the churches and chapels and places of worship were destroyed, and only the poor of the people left in the land, who from their circumstances could not build another.

Charles Ellicott takes the same word as decisive evidence the other way. The expression excludes both meanings the word bore earlier in the psalm, the Temple and the assembly: buildings must be meant, and buildings scattered over the land, which can be nothing but synagogues — the high places would not be called God’s, nor Bethel and Dan, connected as they were with irregular worship. Here then, he says, is a clear note of time, indicating a period not only later than the rise of the synagogue in Ezra’s day but much later, since it takes time for a new institution to spread over a country; and two of the Greek translators actually render the word synagogues. John Wesley is content with the plain description, that these were the public places where the Jews met to worship every sabbath day.
9:
What signs are missed is answered in three ways. John Gill canvasses miracles such as were wrought in Egypt, then prefers the standing ordinances — sabbaths and sacrifices, the passover and circumcision — which were signs of God’s presence and were interrupted in the captivity; Kimchi, he adds, took them for signs of redemption. Charles Ellicott takes the statement in contrast to the heathen signs mentioned earlier: while those abominations were visibly set up as rallying points of savage profanity, the tokens of the invisible God’s presence are no more seen. Adam Clarke reads the complaint and then qualifies it from the history. They have left us no memorial that God has been among us, he paraphrases — but we may say, he adds, that they were not totally destitute even of these, since the preservation of Daniel in the lions’ den and of the three Hebrews in the furnace, the change that came upon Nebuchadnezzar, and the handwriting that appeared to Belshazzar were all evidences that God had not left them without proof of his regard.

Whether there was truly no prophet is where the entry divides. Adam Clarke grants the letter and denies the substance: none among them in that place could tell how long the captivity was yet to endure, but there were prophets in the captivity, Daniel being one, though his prophecies were confined to a single place, and Ezekiel another, among the captives by the river Chebar. What they had not were prophets who went to and fro through the land, preaching repentance. Charles Ellicott uses the same fact to fix the date. The lament was the constant one of a later age and suits no earlier time into which the rest of the psalm would fit, since during the exile Jeremiah and Ezekiel were prophesying and the complaint then took a different form; and the clause about no one knowing how long carries us past Jeremiah, who had given an exact date for the exile’s end. He hears in it rather the widely spread feeling that afterwards inspired the apocalyptic literature, and quotes the prayer lamenting that there is at this time neither prince, nor prophet, nor leader, nor sacrifice, nor place to sacrifice. John Wesley reaches the same conclusion by the shortest road: probably Ezekiel and Jeremiah were dead when the psalm was composed.

The withdrawn hand is explained from dress by two of them. Adam Clarke notes that the outward habit of the easterns had no sleeves, so that the hands and arms were often covered by the folds of the robe and had to be drawn out before anything could be done; the literal sense is, to what time wilt thou draw back thy right hand from within thy bosom. Charles Ellicott says the same, that the verb means returnest, into the ample folds of the Eastern robe, and that the clause is equivalent to asking why God does not pluck out his right hand to consume. John Gill keeps the hand a figure for power, withdrawn when there is not that success in the ministry of the word there formerly was, and when the enemies of religion prosper and gain ground — God seeming all the while like a man who folds his arms or hides his hands in his bosom.

Adam Clarke then does something unusual with the same two verses. Having said elsewhere that the old metrical psalter of Sternhold and Hopkins was made from the original text, he offers these verses as his proof, granting the version harsh and some of its expressions quaint almost to ridicule, yet holding that it hit the true meaning our prose translators missed — and he prints it, down to the couplet asking God to pluck his hand out and be not slack to give his foes a rap.
12:
The turn to consolation is made on a title. Matthew Henry notes that the church speaks as a complex body, the same in every age, and so can call God her King of old, since as Israel’s King he wrought salvation in the midst of the nations, all he did in the government of the world tending towards the salvation of his church. C.H. Spurgeon makes the same claim a plea: Israel acknowledges her King and claims to have been his possession from of old, and each past miracle of grace assures us that he who has begun to deliver will continue to redeem — his deeds of old having been public and wrought in the teeth of his foes, no delusions or make-believes. John Gill renders the opening particle as but God, or verily God, and makes the verse the church’s consolation under all these circumstances. Where the salvation was wrought divides two of them. Charles Ellicott says the phrase means on the great theatre of the world, and that we certainly must not render land instead of earth, since the wonders of Egypt are the theme; Adam Clarke renders it precisely the other way, that God reigned as a king in the midst of our land, dispensing salvation from the centre to every part of the circumference.

What the broken-headed monsters are is the question of the entry. Charles Ellicott answers it as a naturalist. The word for dragons always indicates some aquatic monster and is elsewhere translated whale; about leviathan the minute description of the crocodile in Job leaves no doubt, and so the other creature, an emblem of Egypt, was some great saurian, perhaps the alligator, the word’s derivation favouring that. Besides its abundance, he adds, another fact that led to the crocodile becoming an emblem of Egypt was the adoration paid to it. John Gill takes leviathan for a large fish, generally thought the whale though by some the crocodile, standing for the king of Egypt or Babylon and afterwards for the Romish antichrist, who in one of his characters is a sea beast with many heads. Matthew Henry, Adam Clarke and John Wesley keep it political: Pharaoh was the leviathan, the Egyptians the dragons, fierce and cruel, and the heads were Pharaoh with his chief captains.

Who ate the carcase is settled the same way by nearly everyone, against the versions. Adam Clarke takes the people inhabiting the wilderness for the birds and beasts of prey which fed on the dead bodies the tides had cast ashore, though the Greek and Latin versions instead read that God gave him for meat to the Ethiopians. Charles Ellicott rejects that reading and two others besides, holding that it is the Egyptian corpses thrown up by the Red Sea that are devoured by the wild beasts, which are called people here as the ants and conies are called so elsewhere. John Wesley agrees, finding the name significant, since those creatures are the only people that inhabit the desert.

The cleaving of the rock and the drying of the rivers closes the retrospect. John Gill names the rocks at Horeb and at Kadesh, from which water flowed as out of a fountain, and concludes that God will not suffer his people to want but will open fountains and rivers for them in the wilderness. Adam Clarke asks whether the drying of mighty rivers does not refer to the cutting off of Jordan, so that the people passed over dryshod. John Wesley takes both Jordan and the Red Sea, and defends calling a sea a river on the ground that the same title is expressly given to it by Homer and other ancient writers. Charles Ellicott corrects the nouns: the flood is better rendered brook, and the mighty rivers are perhaps rather rivers of constant flow, which did not dry up in summer as the brooks did.
16:
The day and the night are made to prove different things. John Gill reads them as providence: God made the one and the other and can make them longer or shorter, clear or cloudy, and the day of prosperity and the night of adversity are alike at his disposal — it is now a night of darkness, deadness and security, but ere long there will be no more night, and the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun. He notes that Jarchi took the day for the redemption of Israel and the night for its distresses. Adam Clarke makes the verse an argument from authorship, that God is the author of light and of the sun which dispenses it; and on the following clause he turns to mechanics, saying that God has appointed that peculiarity in the poise and rotation of the earth by which the seasons are produced, and that he alone is the author of all the grand geographical divisions of the globe. John Wesley sums the two clauses as a pair: the one shows God’s power over all places and the next his dominion over all times and seasons. Charles Ellicott traces the wording to the creation narrative, where the same word stands first for the heavenly luminary generally and then for the sun as chief, and glosses the borders of the earth as earth in all directions and to its utmost bounds, as we say from pole to pole. John Gill adds that the bounds fixed include the habitation of every man.

What the psalmist asks God to remember is disputed. John Gill reports that the Greek version paraphrases the clause as remember this thy creation, tying it to what goes before — day and night, light and sun, the borders of the earth, summer and winter — and rejects the connection: the words belong to what follows, and the prayer is that God would remember the enemy and his reproaches, which seemed to be forgotten. Charles Ellicott takes the demonstrative as emphatic and points it backwards after all, since the object of the enemy’s reproach is the Being who has done all these mighty works and is the author of all this wonderful world. John Wesley makes the plea a confession as well: though we deserve to be forgotten, do not suffer our enemies to reproach the name of the great and glorious God. Adam Clarke specifies the reproach, that the heathen not only deny these things but give the honour of them to their false gods, and so blaspheme the name.

Matthew Henry turns the whole passage into an argument for confidence. The cause of religion is God’s own cause and he will certainly plead it, though for a time he seems to neglect it; he will arise and stir up himself and do his own work in his own time. That the cause is his own Henry proves from the character of the persecutors, who are God’s sworn enemies: what is done against his people for his sake does by consequence reflect upon him, but that is not all, since they have directly and immediately reproached him and blasphemed his name, which was what they roared in the sanctuary, triumphing as if they had mastered the God of Israel. And from that he draws a conclusion that runs the other way from grief: as nothing grieves the saints more than to hear God’s name blasphemed, so nothing encourages them more to hope that God will appear against their enemies than when those enemies have arrived at such a pitch of wickedness as to reproach God himself, since this fills the measure of their sins apace and hastens their ruin.
19:
The turtledove is expounded at length by two voices and dissolved by a third. John Gill draws out every point: the church is like the creature for its cleanness and purity, its harmlessness and innocence, its modesty and meekness, its chastity to its mate, its mournful voice when that mate is lost, and its being a timorous, weak thing exposed to the prey of others. John Wesley keeps four of those qualities, simple and harmless, meek and faithful, and Adam Clarke reads the figure as a plea, that God’s people are helpless, defenceless, miserable and afflicted, and should no longer be given over to the power of their brutal adversaries. Charles Ellicott works on the Hebrew instead. One word occurs in both halves of the verse and is presumably used in the same sense, and it may mean life, or animal, or troop; a parallel elsewhere suggests taking it with its neighbour in the sense of a greedy band, which gives: deliver not thy dove to the greedy band, forget not the band of the afflicted for ever.

Which covenant is to be respected divides the next verse. John Wesley takes it for the covenant made with Abraham, by which God gave the land of Canaan to him and to his seed for ever. Adam Clarke takes it for the covenant sacrifice instead, the one Abraham offered when the contracting parties passed through between the separated parts of the victim, which he calls an indisputable type of Jesus Christ and of God and man meeting in his sacrificed humanity.

The dark places are read literally, geographically and by emendation. Adam Clarke means real caves and dens and woods, full of robbers and murderers continually destroying God’s people, so that the holy seed seems as if it would be entirely cut off; and he applies it either way, since Judea was then little else than a den of robbers, its own inhabitants having been removed, while Chaldea was infested with banditti. John Wesley says only that it is the dark and dismal land in which we live. Charles Ellicott objects on the ground of usage: the word rendered habitations is so consistently used of the quiet resting-places of God’s people that it seems quite impossible the psalmist should have written resting-places of cruelty, and a slight change in the text gives instead that they have filled thy land with darkness and thy quiet dwelling with violence.

The closing petitions are given a reason apiece. John Gill reads the oppressed returning ashamed as coming back from the throne of grace without an answer to their prayer, while Adam Clarke takes the return literally and asks that the people be not so diminished that when restored to their own land they should appear but a handful of men. On the last plea John Gill makes the church’s cause the cause of God himself, which he calls a forcible argument for asking him to arise and exert himself, and Adam Clarke names the fool as the idolater, who boasts of the superiority of his idols and asserts that it is by their power we have been brought under their domination — so that in praying for our own salvation we are calling on God to vindicate his own injured honour.
